name: The Moon

orbits.name: Low polar mapping orbit (50 km)
orbits.blurb: Skims the surface for the sharpest data, but lumpy lunar gravity means frequent station-keeping burns.

orbits.name: Polar orbit (100 km)
orbits.blurb: The classic choice: good resolution, modest station-keeping.
orbits.notes: Lunar Prospector's mapping orbit (NSSDCA 1998-001A): near-circular, 100 km, 90° inclination, 118-minute period, re-circularised about once a month. Science modifiers and maintenance Δv are game values.

orbits.name: Frozen elliptical orbit (30 × 200 km)
orbits.blurb: A naturally stable orbit — almost no fuel to maintain, but you only fly low over the south pole.

notes: Verified: GM (JPL SSD), volumetric mean radius 1,737.4 km and the Earth distances (NSSDCA Moon Fact Sheet: semimajor axis 384,400 km, mean perigee 363,300 km, mean apogee 405,500 km). Game-scale estimate, not from a NASA table: radiationKradPerYear.

name: Mars

orbits.name: Low circular polar orbit (300 km)
orbits.blurb: Best for sharp images and radar. Braking straight into it takes a huge burn.

orbits.name: Low circular orbit via aerobraking
orbits.blurb: Capture into a loose orbit, then dip into the atmosphere for ~6 months to shrink it. Saves over 1 km/s of fuel — if the solar panels survive.
orbits.notes: Capture orbit and duration follow Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (NSSDCA 2005-029A): a 400 × 35,000 km capture orbit, then about six months of aerobraking. Science modifiers and maintenance Δv are game values.

orbits.name: Elliptical 'deep dip' orbit (150 × 6,200 km)
orbits.blurb: Swoops through the upper atmosphere to taste escaping gas. Cheaper to reach, worse for photos.

notes: Verified: GM 42,828 km³/s² and volumetric mean radius 3,389.5 km (NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet, JPL SSD); Earth distance min 54.6 and max 401.4 million km (NSSDCA). The mean Earth distance, 1.70 AU, is the time average over 2026-2041 computed from the JPL approximate elements (it is not the 1.52 AU orbit radius). Game-scale estimate: radiationKradPerYear.

name: Jupiter

orbits.name: Polar orbit, 53-day period
orbits.blurb: Dives under the radiation belts at closest approach, then swings far out to recover. Science happens in brief, intense perijove passes.
orbits.notes: Juno's actual orbit after its 5 July 2016 insertion: 53.5-day period, perijove about 4,200 km above the cloud tops (NSSDCA 2011-040A). Radiation and duty-cycle multipliers are game values. Imaging is ×0.9 (game value): close perijove passes give sharp views, as JunoCam showed; at ×0.7 the wide-angle camera could never meet the 0.5 quality bar, so no design could earn the imaging objective.

orbits.name: Polar orbit, 14-day period
orbits.blurb: Nearly 4× more close passes per year — and nearly 4× the radiation. Needs a bigger braking burn.
orbits.notes: Juno's originally planned 14-day science orbit, never flown: the period-reduction burn was cancelled after the October 2016 valve problem (JPL, Feb 2017). Apoapsis chosen to give a 14-day period. Radiation and duty-cycle multipliers are game values. Imaging is ×0.9 (game value): close perijove passes give sharp views, as JunoCam showed; at ×0.7 the wide-angle camera could never meet the 0.5 quality bar, so no design could earn the imaging objective.

notes: Verified: GM 126,687,000 km³/s² and volumetric mean radius 69,911 km (NSSDCA Jupiter Fact Sheet, JPL SSD); Earth distance min 588.5 and max 968.5 million km (NSSDCA). Mean Earth distance 5.26 AU is the time average over 2026-2038 from the JPL approximate elements. Game-scale estimates, not from a NASA table: radiationKradPerYear (dose behind standard shielding in a Juno-like polar orbit, chosen so that a spacecraft needs a vault, as Juno did) and solarArrayExtraDegradationPerYear.
